translation:
A Vaishnav has no meditation other than Vasudev; he considers other gods (anya-dev) and his chosen deity (ishta-dev) as one and the same. Whoever has received the complete grace of Namdev and Kabirji — for him that impurity will be removed.

_Antavat tu phalam teshaam tad bhavaty alpamedhasaam, devaan devayajo yaanti madbhaktaa yaanti maam api_ (Gita 7.23) (Those who do not know the Supreme are of limited understanding, and the fruit they seek is perishable; worshippers of the gods, out of that distinction, go to the gods, but My devotees — however they may worship — ultimately come to Me alone.) (Kalyan, 2nd year, No. 2, p.203)

One day, while in samadhi, Shri Shankaracharya became aware that his aged mother wished to leave her body, and without any delay he came at once to her feet. Seeing her son present beside her, the mother said, "I have grown old; I no longer wish to keep this useless body, so pray to the Lord for my good end (sadgati)." In accordance with his mother's wish, Shri Shankar Swami offered praise (stuti) to Lord Shiva. Pleased, Shiva sent his attendants (gana) to bring Shankaracharya's mother to Shivlok. But the mother said, "Son, I have no desire to go to Shivlok; I wish only to have the vision (darshan) of Lord Vishnu, who bears the conch, discus and mace." She worshipped and adored Lord Vishnu. Shrimannarayana, who is devoted to protecting the distressed and is loving toward His devotees (bhaktavatsal), was pleased and gave Shankaracharya's mother a place in His own abode; and Shankaracharya, having performed his mother's last rites, fulfilled the vow he had earlier made. (Kalyan, 2nd year, No. 1, p.145)

VISHNU BHAKTI

(Najar No. 1, p.130)

This account is found in the biography (jeevan charitra) of Vallabhacharya of the Pushtimarg.

In the Pushtimarg, since one attains Purushottam by offering seva of body (tanuja), wealth (vittaja) and mind (maanasi), the path of bhakti is, on that account, far superior to the path of knowledge (gnanmarg).

The meaning of Pushtimarg is "the path of the Lord's grace (kripa)"; on that path one performs seva or bhakti of the Lord — keeping one's mind (chitt) fixed on Shri Hari is called seva.

_Mahaatmya-gnyaana-purvastu sudridhaah sarvatodhikaa, sneho bhaktir iti proktas tayaa muktir na chaanyathaa_ ||1|| (Pi.Sha.42) (Firm and unshakeable love for the Lord, greater than all else and founded on knowledge of His greatness, is called bhakti; and it is only through bhakti that liberation (mukti) is attained, never otherwise.)

Love (sneh) that is steady, grounded in knowledge of the Lord's greatness (mahatmya), and greater than all other love, is called bhakti; and liberation comes only through bhakti — it comes in no other way. Seva and bhakti are used in one and the same sense.

Maryada Marg — the path in which one performs action (karma), worship (puja) and upasana or bhakti according to the rules laid down in the Smritis and Dharmashastras is called the Maryada Marg. This path includes every path except the Lord's nirgun (attributeless) bhakti. A path in which action or bhakti is performed while remaining bound to injunctions and prohibitions (vidhi-nishedh) is called Maryada; and a path in which, setting aside worldly and Vedic restrictions, one performs exclusive and undivided (ananya-nishkaam) bhakti of the Lord is called Pushtimarg.

VISHNU BHAKTI

In the Samagam, Jivanji Maharaj described three kinds of Vaishnavs: (1) those of the Pravah (flow) path, (2) those of the Pushtimarg, (3) those of the Maryada Marg; and these Vaishnavs are further of three kinds each, according to the nature of the three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas).

In the dharma that Vallabhacharya established in this Kali Yuga, there are 84 nirguni Vaishnavs, 84 rajasic, 84 tamasic, and 84 sattvic — making 252 in all belonging to the three gunas, among whom the nirguni are the best. Their story — the Varta — was told by the fourth Gosainji, Gokulnathji ("Lalji"), to Kalan Bhat; it appears in Manibehn Najar's Samagam, p.74.

Sadguru Jivanji, describing Vaishnavs of a fourth guna beyond the three — those who are trigunatit (transcending the three gunas) — has shown a bhakti free of the three gunas. Those of the Pravah path apply the tilak, sing the praises of Ram's name, undertake pilgrimages and vows, perform yagnas, give charity and merit-making gifts, and take up study and teaching — these are the six kinds of action they perform. Now the text shows what Vishnu bhakti should be like and why it should be practiced.

Pushtimarg has been called the dharma of the Dvapar Yuga. Now, in the Samagam, when describing the Maryada Vaishnavs, the Divine Kala (Jivanji), in describing the dharma of Kali Yuga, narrates an episode concerning the four yugas. In it, the three other yugas, calling Kali Yuga the most base and dull-witted of the four, reproach it before the Lord, saying: "We possess long lifespans, whereas Kali Yuga is of brief lifespan and base intellect; therefore set it apart from us." Then the Lord's reply — the verse from the Nityakshari Mimansa given in the Samagam as the 46th shloka — says: He said, alas, this is a matter of sorrow; who is more excellent than you? Yet the fruit of Kali Yuga is that it does whatever you wish. Commenting on that verse, the Lord says: O Yugas! You, possessors of base intellect, have caused Me great pain by speaking such wicked words; shame, shame upon your dharma — for My kevalya bhakti, that is, My one pure and undivided devotion, resides precisely in Kali Yuga, and it is that Kali Yuga which you scorn. And He said: O Yugas, for Me you are like a single tree, which has flourished in the forms of Satyug, Tretayug and Dvaparyug, and upon which the fruit called Kaliyug has now formed.

_Satyug tretaa dvaaparne, prabhue karyo dhikkaar, param bhagat kaliyug chhe, nirgun bhakti prakaash_ (The Lord reproached Satyug, Treta and Dvapar; the supreme devotee is Kaliyug — it is the manifestation of nirgun bhakti.)

_Dhyaayan krite japen mantrais tretaayaam dvaapare architan, yad aapnoti tad aapnoti kalau sankirtya keshavam_ (Kalyan Bhakti Ank, p.430, 6.1.17, Vishnu Purana) (What was obtained in Satyug through meditation, in Treta through recitation of mantras, and in Dvapar through worship — that same fruit is obtained in Kaliyug simply through the kirtan of Keshav's name.)

_Krite yad dhyaayato Vishnum, tretaayaam yajato makhaih, dvaapare paricharyaayaam, kalau tad Harikirtanaat_ (Bhagavat) (The fruit that comes to one who meditates on Vishnu in Satyug, to one who worships Vishnu through yagnas in Treta, and to one who serves Vishnu in Dvapar — that same fruit is obtained in Kaliyug simply by singing the kirtan of Shri Hari.)

_Kaler doshanidhe rajan asti hy eko mahaan gunah, kirtanaad eva Krishnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet_ ||51|| (Skandh 12, Adhyay 3) (O King Parikshit! In Kaliyug, a storehouse of faults, there is one great virtue — that merely by the kirtan of Shri Krishna, the soul, freed from bondage, attains the supreme state.)

_Tapah param kritayuge, tretaayaam gnyaanam uchyate, dvaapare yagyam evaahur, gaanam ekam kalau yuge_ (Parashar Samhita, Adhyay 1, Shloka 22) (In Kaliyug there is no efficacy left in yoga, yagna or knowledge — the singing of the praises of Ramchandraji is the only support.)

_Ekaakaaram kalim drishtvaa saaravat saaraniirasam, Vishnu-raatah sthaapitavaan kalijaanaam sukhaaya cha_ ||69|| (Bhagavat Mahatmya, Adhyay 1) (Seeing that in Kaliyug bhakti alone is the means, and that knowledge, dispassion and the rest have become tasteless for the soul, for the happiness of the people of Kaliyug, Vishnurat (Shukdevji) established that through bhakti alone will a person cross over this world.)

_Satyaaditri-yuge bodha-vairaagyau mukti-saadhakau, kalau tu kevalaa bhaktir brahma-saayujya-kaarini_ ||4|| (Bhagavat Mahatmya, Adhyay 2) (In the three yugas beginning with Satyug, knowledge and dispassion were the means to liberation; in Kaliyug, bhakti alone grants union with Brahma — moksha.)

_Na preto na pishaacho vaa raakshaso vaasuro'pi vaa, bhakti-yukta-manaskaanaam sparshane na prabhur bhavet_ ||17|| (Bhagavat Mahatmya, Adhyay 2) (No ghost, no evil spirit, no demon and no asura has the power to touch those great souls (mahatmas) whose minds are devoted to bhakti.)

_Etan nirvidyamaanaanaam icchhataam akutobhayam, yoginaam nripa nirnitam Harer naamaanukirtanam_ ||11|| (Skandh 2, Ansh 1) (O king! For those who are utterly dispassionate, seeking that state where fear can arise from nowhere (akutobhayam) — even for great yogis desiring that state — it is settled that the kirtan of Hari's name alone is the way; whoever, through yogic practice, wishes to reach that supreme state, for him the kirtan of the Lord's name has been declared the only means; there is no other means besides this. Or: the great yogis who desired that fearless supreme state determined that the sole means of crossing this world is the kirtan of the Lord's name.)

_Kali sabhajayanty aaryaa guna-gnyaah saara-bhaaginah, yatra sankirtanenaiva sarvah svaartho'bhilabhyate_ ||36|| (Skandh 11, Adhyay 5) (Discerning, virtue-knowing great souls praise Kaliyug more than the other three yugas, because in Kaliyug both worldly and spiritual ends (swarth and paramarth) are attained through sankirtan alone.)

_Shuddhah Kaliyugah smritah_ (Manusmriti, Adhyay 1, Shloka 86) (Kaliyug is remembered as pure.)

_Raameti varnadvayam aadarena sadaa smaran muktim upaiti jantuh, kalau yuge kalmasha-maanasaanaam anyatra vrittir na khalu naadhikaarah_ (By always remembering, with reverence, the two syllables "Ram," beings attain liberation. In Kaliyug, for those of impure disposition, truly there is no other authority — no other means — for liberation.)

_Kabir satjug sat treheta tap, dvaapar puja samaai, kalime keval naam hai, sat lok mili jaay_ (Kabir says: in Satyug there was truth, in Treta austerity, in Dvapar worship — but in Kaliyug there is only the Name; through it one merges with the true realm, Satlok.)

Pujya Yadunath wrote a letter in Samvat 2005, Jeth Sud 13, to the devotee Tribhovan Ramkrishna of Jaipur, in which he wrote: "Brother, this is Kaliyug; it suits the fit practitioner but is unfavourable to Gokul (physical maya). Kaliyug is also called Namyug, the age of the Name, in which the soul's welfare (atma-kalyan) is quickly accomplished through the Lord's name."

The praise of Kaliyug given in shlokas 46-47 is supported both in the Bhagavat and in the words of every saint. It is said too in Krishnadas's Parichari:

_Satjugme sat-bhakti karahi, treyaame tap hu anusarahi, dvaaparme puja aachaaraa, kaljugme ek naam aadhaaraa_ (In Satyug, devotion was performed through truthfulness; in Treta, the practice of austerity was followed; in Dvapar, worship and ritual observance (puja-achar) were carried out; but in Kaliyug, bhakti rests on the support of the Name alone.)

Regarding the dharma of devotion: Sadguru Jivanji, after examining the religions across the whole of India, determined and firmly established what should be called true Vishnu bhakti. One can gauge how much effort Sadguru Jivanji must have made in searching for this supreme truth from the wondrous shlokas given in the Samagam — from where, and with how much labour, Jivanji must have distilled the essence of so many shastras, puranas and vedas, one will understand. Here, for instance, shloka 45 is a proof-text taken from the Nityakshari verse found in the Mimansa. Thus Jivanji consulted the Vedas and other great texts as well — texts of which today we cannot even conceive. This, then, is one of Jivanji's great achievements.

Regarding Kaliyug, he determined that in Kaliyug there is no dharma other than the kirtan and remembrance (smaran) of Vishnu alone. Further, in shloka 48, drawn from the Parashar Smriti, Parashar too stated what conduct should not be practiced in Kaliyug, and also showed whose opinion is acceptable in this Kaliyug. The Vedas, Shastras and Puranas have indeed all pointed only to Vishnu bhakti; but for the sake of worldly enjoyment (bhog) and material pleasures, people cling to the path of worship of other gods (anya-dev), yagnas and such ritualistic (saakam) karmakand. Seeing all this, Jivanji Maharaj, in order to bring about the soul's welfare, established the Uda Dharma to promote the path in which exclusive (ananya) bhakti alone is the sole means. In shloka 48, by giving the verse of Parashar's Smriti, Jivanji showed that even the shastras and sages support his own view. In this shloka, Parashar indicated certain acts not to be performed in Kaliyug — he lists five such acts that should not be done: (1) agnikshetra (fire-rites), (2) cow-slaughter (gau-vadh), (3) sannyas (renunciation), (4) shraddha (ancestor-rites) performed with meat, and (5) begetting a son through a brother-in-law (devar). These five have been declared forbidden (varjya) in Kaliyug. The translation of this shloka is given below, as it is stated in verse:

_Agnikshetra sanyaasaru, mukha panukhand hai, devarsachaat piitiru, aamish nind hai, so ya kalime naahi, kahe adh dhaam hai, unchitaa Krishn ik naam, gaamko naam hai_ (These practices are not to be done in this Kaliyug; they are said to belong to a base abode; instead one should uplift oneself through the one name of Krishna — that is the true name of the village of dharma.)

The Nirnaya-Sindhu and other texts have also discussed the five prohibitions of Kaliyug. Naradji, though counted among the Vaishnavs, also taught that yagna should not be performed. Originally, the Vaishnavs were those who upheld the dharma of compassion (daya-dharma); among them, those who became atheistic accepted karma as the cause of the world. In ancient times five kinds of acts were current, which, regarding their prohibition in Kaliyug, are stated below according to the words of the sage Parashar: (1) agnikshetra, (2) sannyas, (3) cow-slaughter in yagna, (4) devaravat — begetting a son through the devar (niyog), (5) shraddha should not be performed with meat.

_Agnikshetraam gavaalambha sanyaasam palapaitukam, devaraashtomam sutotpati kalau panth vivarjayet_ ||48|| (Samagam) (Agnikshetra, cow-slaughter, sannyas, the eating of meat at shraddha, and begetting a son through the devar — this path should be abandoned in Kaliyug.)

Agnikshetra means the killing of cows; sannyas and eating meat at shraddha, and marrying a widow to the devar. It appears that the reason agnikshetra was stopped was to stop violence (himsa). This is because, once agnikshetra is undertaken, animal-sacrifice (pashu-yaag) follows from it; hence, with the intent of stopping violence, its very root was cut away, it seems. "Gavalambh" means the slaughter of cows; this is written at length in the Vedas. In the Bhagavat, the word "aalambhan" should be understood to mean an offering to the gods (devarpan), not slaughter — so it is written there. Up to the Manu and Yajnavalkya Smritis, gavalambh was retained; after that, it is written of in the Puranas and in the Narad text as well. So this prohibition was not made many years ago. It is written that one should not take sannyas in Kaliyug, the reason being that in this age people would take sannyas and then cause disturbance and hypocrisy — and that is exactly what has happened. Many sannyasis follow the leftist (vamamargi) path and are hypocrites (dhongi); they do not truly keep the ascetic's dharma at all, and instead become greedy. As for "palapaitruk" — eating meat at shraddha for the sake of the ancestors (pitru) — it appears that in ancient times all people were meat-eaters and lived by hunting; they would bring back the animals they killed, offer them to the gods, and eat the remainder — this was the custom in the Vedic age. Afterward, in the time of the Smritis, this custom fell into disuse, to the extent that no one ate meat except on the occasions prescribed by ritual. It appears that this was codified in the Smritis; then came the Puranas, in which too permission for eating meat in rituals is found — so the Vaishnavs regard such Puranas as tamasic, and the Puranas that establish the dharma of compassion they call sattvic. Regarding shraddha, the Sindhu text writes:

_Yatra maatulajo dvaahi yatra vaishvalii-patih, shraaddham na gacchhet dviprakritam yasya niraamisha_ ||1|| (One should not go to eat shraddha-food at the house of a man who has married his maternal uncle's daughter, or who has married the daughter of a shudra woman.)

Originally, the meaning of the funeral rite was this: with the thought "who will feed the one who has died?", the relatives would offer water and pinda (rice-balls), believing that this would satisfy the deceased's hunger and thirst, and that the deceased would thereby become content; and upon this the Brahmins built up an elaborate system, devising the thirteenth-day (teradashi), monthly and yearly shraddha rites, and introducing many kinds of gifts (dan) into them. In some wild regions, when someone dies, money is tied into a cloth at the corpse's edge, and then it is cremated — that, it seems, was the original Hindu custom, which was reformed to produce the funeral rite (antyeshti karma) as now written. Looking at the original Ashvalayan Sutra, this ritual is seen to be brief, and there is no period of sutak (ritual impurity) at all in it. As for niyog — begetting a son on the field, that is, the wife, through appointment of another man — this prohibition now appears in the texts as a prohibition of gotra; it seems this prohibition occurred at that time. In the Rigveda Samhita, in the seventh Ashtak, eighth Adhyay, eighteenth Varg, there is a passage about devarotpatti (begetting through the devar); that mantra is written below:

_Kau vaa shaputra vidhave vade varam marya nayaashaakrinute sathasya aa_. Nirukta: _Devarah kasmaad dvitiyo vara uchyaate_. It is written in the Aitareya Brahmana — _Naikasyaa bahavah sahapatayah_ — with the gloss: "sah" means the prohibition ordained is against simultaneous plurality of husbands, not against sequential remarriage.

Meaning: a woman should not take more than one husband at the same time, but there is no bar to her taking another husband if the first has died.

In the Dravid country there are two sects — the Ramanuj Brahmins of the Dravid country have two sects, "Tengale" and "Vadagale"; among these, the Tengale Brahmins have abandoned Vedic practice. There is no statement in the Shruti or Smriti regarding tonsuring (vapan) a widow's head.

_Vidhvad-vipra-nripah striinaam neshyato keshm vaapanam, sarvaan keshaan samuddhritya chhedyed anguladvayam, evam naari kumariinaam shiraso mundana smritam_. Yam, Parashar, Apastamb and the Gita have declared: _Yagyo daanam tapash chaiva paavanaani maniishinaam_ (Yagna, giving (dan), and austerity (tap) are the purifying acts for the wise.) Yagna means worship of God, dan means benevolence toward others, tap means restraint of the senses — these are the principal meanings; but when sectarian pride arises, people twist these meanings to suit their convenience. The original meaning of karma was worship of the deity, but its outcome came to rest on cruelty; likewise, gnyan (knowledge) means recognizing the one God, setting aside the many gods, and maintaining an equal vision (samdrishti) through compassion for all beings — this became corrupted, and paths like Aghori, Kaul and Vam (left-hand tantra) emerged from within the path of knowledge, so that the true purpose of that path was lost. Likewise bhakti means worship of God (Ishwar-upasana), but in its place thousands of imagined gods came into being. Tap means control of the senses, but in its place emerged those who hold their arms upright, stand on one leg, or perform the five-fires austerity (panchagni-tap), so the true purpose of tap too was lost.

In Nadiad, the carpenter community resolved not to have their funeral rites performed by their usual priest, because even after paying money, the priest would not release them from further demands.

The meaning of "the knower" (gnyani) is given as follows in the Narayana Upanishad:

_Tasyaiva vidusho yagyasyaatmaa yajamaanah shraddhaa patni shariram ivandhah, hridayam yoopah kaam aajyam manyuh pashuh tapo'gnir dagdhah shamayitaa_ ||1|| (How the meaning of "the knower" comes about, in detail: the self (atma) is the performer of the yagna; the heart is the sacrificial post (yup), that is, the stake to which the animal is tied; and our faith (shraddha) is the wife; the ghee needed for the offering is our own desire (vasana); the animal needed for the sacrifice is our anger; the fire needed is our own austerity (tap); and the one who slays the animal is our own discernment (dam, i.e. viveka).) This Upanishad contains much further detail of this kind; its name is Pranagnihotra.

Worshipping through bhakti satisfies the Supreme Lord (Bhagavat, Skandh 5, Adhyay 5, Shloka 23).

_Yasmin nribhih prahutam shraddhayaaham ashnaami kaamam tathaagnihotre_ ||23|| (I am satisfied by the worship offered with faith through bhakti; it does not happen through agnikshetra.)

_Yathaa taror mula-nishechanena trishyanti tat-skandha-bhujopashaakhaah, praanopahaaraach cha yathendriyaanaam tathaiva sarvaarhanam achyutejyaa_ ||2|| (By worshipping the one God, all the gods are thereby satisfied — just as, by watering the root of a tree, all its branches are satisfied, and just as, by putting food into the stomach, all the senses are satisfied — so it is with worship of the Lord.) (Bhagavat)

_Raamanaamnaiva muktih syaat kalau naanyena kenachit, vipraad adishtagunayutaad aravindavimukhaah shvapachovarishtham_ ||3|| (In Kaliyug, there is no dharma other than worshipping the Lord through His Name; if a learned Brahmin and a devotee from a historically outcaste community (dhed) are compared, and the latter is a devotee, then the devotee should be considered the greater — just as, if there are fifty large and powerful buffaloes and their herdsman is an eight-year-old boy, the animals still flee out of fear of his stick.)

One-God doctrine — from the Vedas, Shastras and Puranas, the settled conclusion is that God is one; but on the conventional (rudhi) path no one accepts this — people worship thousands of gods, though with their mouths they say there is one, in practice treating Him as separate from those thousands.

Shiv-puja, Vishnu-puja — Vaishnavs do not accept that Shiva's worship should be performed in the form of the linga; they do not take darshan of the linga or accept prasad at that pilgrimage-place. If they go to Kashi, they do not take darshan of Vishveshwar (Shiva); and although people go to Hinglaj Mata, where the Gosai ascetics go for darshan, Vaishnavs of all four sampradayas do not go there. The reason is that violence (himsa) takes place before that Mother deity, so, they say, we do not take her darshan. Sahajanand Swami has written in the Shikshapatri that a Satsangi should not take darshan of any deity to whom honey or meat is offered. Those of the Pushtimarg — both the maryaadi and the samarpani — practice exclusive (ananya) bhakti, and regard the linga as unfit for worship.

Four Sampradayas — the Vaishnavas' four principal sampradayas are: (1) Ramanuj, (2) Nimbark, (3) Madhva, (4) Vishnuswami. All four propagated the doctrine of dvait (dualism) and refuted the advait (non-dualist) view propagated by Shankaracharya.

To be Heard but Not Practiced — it is said in the Bharat scripture: "_Dharmasya tattvam nihitam guhaayaam, mahaajano yena gatah sa panthaah_" (The essence of dharma lies hidden in a secret place; the path is that upon which the great saints have walked.)

People's faith in convention (rudhi) is so firmly fixed that if anyone acts even slightly against convention, an outcry is raised against them. The force of convention is such that although the belief among Vaishnavs is that yagna should not be performed in a temple, the temple is in fact sanctified through the recitation (parayan) of the Vedas, in which the procedures for yagna, ashvamedh, naramedh and other rites are recited — and this is considered highly meritorious to hear. Yet the rule is: hear it, but do not perform it. Then a great question arises — is there merit or not in hearing the recitation of a rite one is not permitted to perform?

_Krishna bhogi shukatyaagi raajaa janaka-raaghavau, vasishtha karmakartaa cha panchaite samagnyaaninah_ ||4|| (Krishna the enjoyer, Shuka the renunciate, King Janak, Raghav (Ram), and Vasishtha the performer of rites — these five are equally counted as men of knowledge.)

If, in the same way, everyone gave up their prescribed work and, merely carrying on their own occupations, became knowers (gnyani), what harm would there be? But people say that since it is not the convention, one must take sannyas. Yet, by that logic, when did Krishna, Ram or Janak ever take sannyas? People call the mendicant (bava) a guru, yet on the one hand they will not even drink water touched by him, thinking themselves to belong to a pure, known caste, regarding the bava and sadhu as impure, whose water should not be drunk — while on the other hand they believe that this same bava will send them to moksha. There is, then, no consistency whatever in this according to convention.

Idol Worship — the worship of images arose from the Tantras and Puranas, but it is nowhere found in the Vedas. In rites such as sandhya and brahma-yagna there is no image. Once the path of image-worship emerged, it gave people great licence. From sect to sect, in village after village and in the wilds, many images came into being — one sect made an image, and then another made a different one; some with four arms, some with eight, some with ten, some with four faces, some with six faces; some of peaceful form, some of a warrior, some of a woman, some of animals, some half-animal and half-human — and thereafter came their worship, their vehicles, vessels, weapons, ornaments and adornments, their families and their extent, their servants and attendants, their queens, and so on — all this was constructed, and because of it the Hindu people fell into great delusion and darkness.

(The exposition from Nigam Prakash ends here.)

The Gruhyagni-karma-prayogmala discusses forbidden acts (nishiddha karma). It states: "See the commentary at the end of the Paraskara Grihyasutra, Kanda 3, Kandika 2, where verses of the Harihar Smriti are quoted:

_Asvargyam loka-vidvishtam dharmam apy aacharen na tu_ (One should not follow even a nominal dharma that is not conducive to heaven and is despised by the world) (thus it is remembered in the Smriti); and:

_devaren sutotpattir vaanaprasthaashram-aagrahah, dattaakshataayaah kanyaayaah punardaanam varasya cha, samudra-yaana-sviikaarah kamandalu-vidhaaranam, mahaaprasthaan-gamanam gopashush cha saparaagrahah, agnihotra-havanyaash cha lodho lidhaaparigrahah, asavarnaasu kanyaasu vivaahash cha dvijaatishu, vritta-svaadhyaaya-saapekshaam aghasaad tenanthataa, asthi-sanchayaanaad adhvarmangas parshanam eva cha, praayashchittaabhidhaanam cha vipraanaam maranaantikam, sansarga-doshah paapeshu madhuparke pashor vadhaah, dattauraso'shaantu putratvon parigrahah, shaamitram chaiva vipraanaam somavikrayaanan tathaa, dirghakaalaam brahmacharyam naramedhaashvamedhaako, kalauyuge tv imaan dharmaan varjyaan aahur maniishinah_ ||2|| (thus it is remembered in the Smriti)."

If a dharma is opposed to attaining heaven, and is opposed by the world, one should not follow that dharma either. And:

1. Begetting a son through a devar. 2. Taking up the vanaprastha ashram. 3. Giving an already-betrothed, virgin daughter to another groom. 4. Travelling by sea (samudrayaan, ship). 5. Bearing the kamandalu (that is, taking sannyas). 6. Undertaking mahaprasthan (departing by falling from a mountain peak to give up one's life, etc.). 7. Gopashu (a cattle-related rite). 8. Accepting liquor (madya). 9. Licking the residue of an agnihotra offering. 10. Re-licking the already-licked agnihotra offering-vessel. 11. Marriage among the three varnas into another varna's daughters. 12. Reducing prescribed penance (prayashchit) on grounds of good conduct and Vedic study. 13. Touching a limb of the body after the gathering of bones following cremation. 14. Prescribing a Brahmin's penance to last until death. 15. The fault of association (sansarg-dosh) in sins. 16. Killing an animal in the madhuparka-puja. 17. Declaring someone other than an adopted or biological son as one's son. 18. The shaamitra rite for Brahmins (offering, or touching, of an animal in a yagna). 19. Selling the soma-creeper. 20. Lifelong celibacy (naishthik brahmacharya). 21. Naramedh (human sacrifice) and Ashvamedh (horse sacrifice) — these twenty-one dharmas have been declared forbidden in Kaliyug by the sages. Likewise:

_Ashvaalambham gavaalambham sanyaasam palapaitrukam, devaraachcha sutotpattim kalau pancha vivarjayet_ ||1|| (This Parashar Smriti verse also forbids five acts.) 1. Ashvalambh (horse-sacrifice), 2. Gavalambh (cow-sacrifice), 3. Sannyas, 4. Palapaitruk (rites for the ancestors performed with meat), and 5. Begetting a son through the devar.

Here too, among the household rites, there are the second-ashtaka and other rites in which the use of meat and liquor is prescribed in the sutras themselves, but both these acts are forbidden in Kaliyug; therefore, in such cases, we too have used vegetables in place of meat and milk in place of liquor. Wherever such prohibited acts occur in Kaliyug's prescribed rites, one should accomplish the rite using another, permitted substance instead — there is no fault in this. This, in brief, is the conclusion here.

According to the rule of niyog, obtaining a son through another man used to be practiced; that rule was stopped in Kaliyug. Among us there may have been a provision for obtaining a son through the devar; that has been stopped. But let us analyze the word "devar" — devarah, meaning "second husband" (dvitiyo varah) — even that is not proper; in the same way, we say that a sister-in-law (saali) is "half a wife" — that too is not proper. In Kaliyug, vices arise, and they must be kept in restraint. In the Samagam, by giving the birth-related verse of the Parashar Smriti, support has been given for proper conduct, and thereby the objection of the three yugas that scorned Kaliyug has been set aside in this way. In the Vaishnav Dharma Ratnakar too, on page 11, shloka 29, this same Parashar Smriti verse is given. There is a shloka stating which sage's opinion should be accepted in each of the four yugas:

_Krite tu maanavaa dharmaas tretaayaam gautamaah smritaah, dvaapare shankha-likhitau kalau paaraasharasmritih_ ||5|| (In Satyug, the Manu Dharmashastra is authoritative for human beings. In Tretayug, conduct should follow the Gautam Dharmashastra's injunctions. In Dvaparyug, conduct follows the injunctions of Shankh-Likhit; and in Kaliyug, the Dharmashastra is as given according to the opinion of the Parashar Smriti.)

Kaliyug is decried on account of its faults, such as tyranny (atyachar) and misconduct (duracharya); yet within it lies one great virtue — that in this age liberation can be attained through bhakti to Hari's name alone. With reference to this Kaliyug, Jivanji's opinion regarding Kaliyug is given as a sakhi in the Samagam.

_Kaljug aayo Jivanaa, nirgun bhakti prakaash, satjug tretaa dvaapar, karma dhaamki aash_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: now Kaliyug has come, and in this age the sublime bhakti free of the three gunas (nirgun bhakti) holds preeminence, whereas in the ages of Satyug, Treta and Dvapar it was the ritualistic (karmakand) forms of worship that were foremost.) For this sakhi, Trikamdas Gordhandas has composed the following kundali:

_Kaljug aayo Jivanaa, nirgun bhakti prakaash, satjug tretaa dvaapar, karma dhaamki aash. Karma dharmaki aash, trane jug karine pharataa, kaliyug nirgun naam samajhelaa jamthi na daratam, samje sadguru naa daas, samje na jiiv maayaa tanaa, nirgun bhakti prakaash, kaljug aayo Jivanaa_.

Jivanji Maharaj says: now Kaliyug has come, an age that bestows a bhakti free of the three gunas, transcending them altogether (trigunatit), whereas in Satyug, Treta and Dvapar, devotion accompanied by ritual observance (karmakand) was practiced. Thus, while people wandered through the three yugas cherishing devotion through ritual, in Kaliyug there is the Lord's Name, which is beyond the gunas — those who have understood this are not bound by the fetters that Yamraj places upon those bound by karma, for Yamraj cannot cast such a bond upon them; hence they hold no fear of Yama's torment. But the secret of such bhakti can be understood only by the servants of the Sadguru; those souls caught up in the sensory desires (vishay-vaasana) of Maya cannot understand this secret — that this Kaliyug has come to manifest a bhakti free of gunas (nirgun bhakti) for those who can grasp it. So Jivanji has stated.

After discussing how, in the three earlier yugas, japa, tapa, vrat and worship of images held importance, while in Kaliyug bhakti to Hari alone holds the highest place, Jivanji next describes what form and colour God takes in each yuga.

_Satjugmaa Hari shvet the, treheta maa Hari piit, dvaaparmaa Hari shyaamvarn, kaljug rup viparit_ (Jivanji Maharaj says: at the time of Satyug, God's manifestation was white in colour; in Treta, God's hue was yellow; and in Dvapar, God's hue was dark (shyam); but in Kaliyug, God's hue is something quite different, indeed the reverse — strange, as if false, unrecognizable.)

Jivanji has given a shloka as testimony (sakhi) regarding the Lord's form in the three yugas; it is as follows:

_Kathyate varnanaamaabhyaam, shuklah satyayuge harih, raktah shyaamah kramaat krishnah, tretaayaam dvaapare kalau_ (In Satyug, God's colour is white; in Treta, red; in Dvapar, dark (shyam); and in Kaliyug, the Lord's colour is described as Krishna, dark/black.)

Trigun — according to sattva, rajas and tamas, God assumes colour in Satyug, Treta and Dvapar according to the yuga. In the Bhagavat, there is a shloka in which Vasudev speaks of Krishna's colour:

_Sattvam trilokasthitaye svamaayayaa, bibharshi shuklam khalu varnam aatmanah, sargaaya raktam rajasopabrimhitam, krishnam cha varnam tamasaa janaatyaye_ ||20|| (O Lord! At the time of protecting the three worlds, by Your own maya, through the sattva guna, You bear a white form — the nourishing form of Vishnu. At the time of creation of the three worlds, by rajoguna, You bear a red form, augmented — that is, the creative form of Brahma. And at the time of dissolution, by tamoguna, You bear a dark (Krishna) form — the destructive form of Rudra.)

Gargacharya, in the Bhagavat, spoke of Krishna's colour thus:

_Aasan varnaas trayo hy asya grihnato'nuyugam tanuuh, shuklo raktas tathaa piita idaanim krishnataam gatah_ ||13|| _Praagayam Vasudevasya kvachij jaatas tavaatmajah, Vaasudeva iti shrimaan abhignyaah samprachakshate_ ||14|| _Bahuni santi naamaani ruupaani cha sutasya te, gunakarmaanuruupaani taany aham vedano janaah_ ||15|| (Gargacharya said: your son, taking on a body in each yuga, has already had three colours — white, red and yellow — and now he has attained the colour Krishna, dark; that is, he has been born in the form of Krishna. Formerly he was, on an earlier occasion, born as your son, Vasudev's, and the wise call him by the great name Vasudev. Your son has many names and forms, corresponding to his qualities and deeds; those names and forms even I do not fully know, nor do people in general know them.)

_Tad uktam Gargena Nandam prati: kakaarah kamalaakaantaa rikaaro raama ity api, shakaarah shadgunapati shvetadviipa-nivaasakrit_ ||1|| _Nakaaro Naarasinho'yam makaaro hy aksharo'gnibhuk, visargau cha tathaa hy etau naranaaraayana-rishii_ ||2|| _Sampraliinaash cha shat purnaa yasmin shabde mahaamunau, paripurnatame saakshaat kena krishna prakiirtitah_ ||3|| (In the name "Krishna," the letter "ka" is the form of Lakshmiji; "ri" is the form of Ram; "sha" is the form of the God dwelling on the Shveta-dvip (White Island); and "na" is the form of Narasimha. In this way, these six complete forms merge and become perfectly whole in the great sage — the knower — in whom this word dwells; that is, from whose portion (amsh) all these incarnations arise; and he is given the name "Krishna.")

_Vaasavash choendriyaani tad-devaash chittam eva hi, tasmin cheshtate so'pi vaasudeva iti smritah_ (The senses are called "vasu"; their overlord is the chitt (mind), and He who dwells within it and moves it is called Vaasudev.) _Vaasudevo'yam brahmeti shrutish cha_ (There is also a Vedic statement that Vaasudev is none other than Brahman itself.)
